**Our Two Print Proofs**

Every job goes through two proofs before it goes to press: a screen proof, then a paper proof. Each one catches a different kind of problem.

**1. Screen proof: check the words**

The screen proof is a digital copy of the job viewed on a monitor. Use it to read every word carefully and catch spelling errors, typos and other text mistakes. Text is easy to fix at this stage, and a corrected screen proof can be produced immediately at no material cost.

**2. Paper proof: check the ink on the stock**

The paper proof is printed on the actual stock the job will run on. A screen gives off its own light, so it can't show how the ink will look on paper. Ink sits on paper differently depending on the stock: colors may look darker, duller or warmer than on screen. Use the paper proof to confirm that the colors, images and overall appearance look right on the real material.

**Why this order**

We finalize the text first because it's quick and cheap to change on screen. If we made the paper proof first, any spelling fix found afterward would mean printing another paper proof, which costs stock, ink and time. By the time we make a paper proof, the wording should already be settled, so that proof can focus only on how the job looks in print.

**Our Two Print Proofs**

Every job goes through two proofs before it goes to press. Each one catches a different kind of problem, so we always do them in the same order.

**1. Screen proof: check the words**

The first proof is on screen. Use it to read every line of text for spelling errors, typos, missing words and wrong names, numbers or dates. Read slowly, and read the small print as carefully as the headlines.

Do not judge color on the screen proof. A monitor glows with its own light and mixes color differently from ink on paper, so the color you see is only an approximation.

**2. Paper proof: check the ink on the stock**

The second proof is printed on the actual paper or card the job will use. It shows how the ink really looks on that stock: color, darkness, sharpness and how the ink sits on the surface. The same ink can look brighter on coated stock and duller or softer on uncoated stock. Check that colors match what the customer expects, that images and fine detail are clear, and that nothing looks muddy or washed out.

**Why this order**

Text corrections are cheap to make on screen and expensive to make on paper. If we find a spelling mistake after the paper proof, we have to fix it and print another paper proof, which wastes stock, ink and time. So we fix the words first on screen. Once the text is final, the paper proof only has to answer one question: does it look right on the real material?
